brief.label: project brief
brief.text: Cheggout is an ad-tech company partnered with 20+ PSU banks in India. They reached us out to redesign the white-label marketplace SDK they integrate within banking apps.

cells: Cheggout powers major private banks and institutions in India

content.label: THE IDEA
paragraphs: Cheggout enables banks to activate and retain customers with an interactive and gamified marketplace SDK which they integrate within the banks’ existing mobile applications. They wanted a user experience and interface revamp which ensured customer interacts and completes actions within the app. They wanted us to simplify existing userflow and create assets to resonate with the banking audience and their expectations from modern banking/commerce apps.

blocks.text: This project involved understanding user motivations and what drives them. Cheggout had information clusters that helped them understand behaviour of customer segments. Our job was to ensure users who landed on the SDK interacted with the intended sections. Cheggout helps banks boost card value, drive activation, grow usage, and achieve measurable business growth. Our job was to use our UX and UI design experience to ensure the app SDK did as promised.

Since Cheggout’s SDK integrates with multiple banks, each with their guidelines, we had to ensure what we designed could be easily optimized for each individual bank’s app. So, we began with a skeletal frame which clearly laid out the userflow and built on top of that. This helped us keep the experience uniform across all the banking apps, while making minimal changes to the UI elements so that the app SDK was customized enough for the bank but the experience remained the same.

The SDK led to 46% more debit card and mobile app activations and banks saw six times more digital payments. User engagement grew by four times and retained three times more than before the app was integrated.

brief.label: project brief
brief.text: Barebone Collective reached out to us to build the backend of a web application for Amazon Prime Video’s 2026 Father’s Day campaign ‘Watch with Papa’.

video.title: WATCH WITH PAPA | HAPPY FATHER's DAY | ft @Puravjha_, Dalip Tahil, @aatmeme

blocks.text: The web app helped kids schedule the one thing dads really want - time together.

items: Pick a favourite show or movie on Prime Video
Choose a date and time to watch it with your father

blocks.text: It also had the following add-on fun activities:

The frontend was designed by Barebones Collective and developed with Loveable. Our task was to add the functionality layer and build a robust backend to handle the expected traffic during the campaign. While the application was a standalone system, the features like booking tickets, add-ons and generating the personalized ticket mimicked the theatre booking experience everyone is used to. So, we had to ensure the backend was built to support the frontend experience at all times. And given the audience base of Amazon Prime Video, we had to optimize the backend to cater them all.

One of the challenges was ensuring the application worked without storing any user data. The brief stated users should be able to access and generate tickets without having to create an account or sign in to the application. Since the application lets users book more than one ticket, listing all tickets was a ‘must-have’ feature. Without having a database to associate users to their activity within the app was a challenge. We found a way around the no-database policy by storing the ticket booking information on the users’ local storage which ensured they found all tickets they booked when they accessed the application from the same browser.

We finished the project in 5 days, including multiple cups of coffee and rounds of tweaking and testing the backend to ensure Prime video subscribers loved the experience as much as we and our pals at Barebones Collective did.
All and all, it was a fun experience for us. And for us, it was the first exposure to adding a backend to an AI generated frontend.

blogPosts.title: Are Designers Just Copycats? The Truth About UX Originality
blogPosts.subtitle: Are designers just copying each other? A look at design patterns, tradition, and why originality in UX often builds on what already works.

body.html: Has tradition become performative? Culture today seems to live under constant pressure to stay relevant. Rituals are reshaped, symbols are polished, and heritage is neatly packaged for modern audiences. Traditions quietly shift to match trends, tastes, and whatever the moment demands. What once moved naturally from one generation to the next now arrives curated and market ready. In the name of keeping tradition alive, people have found rather profitable ways to redesign it.
body.text: Has tradition become performative? Culture today seems to live under constant pressure to stay relevant. Rituals are reshaped, symbols are polished, and heritage is neatly packaged for modern audiences. Traditions quietly shift to match trends, tastes, and whatever the moment demands. What once moved naturally from one generation to the next now arrives curated and market ready. In the name of keeping tradition alive, people have found rather profitable ways to redesign it.

body.html: And in many ways, this is inevitable. Time changes things. People change with it. What one generation treats as sacred, the next generation edits, alters, and reshapes to suit its own moment. Traditions bend, meanings shift, and ideas slowly pick up new shapes as they pass through different hands. Creative work has always moved like this. Artists look at what came before them, borrow from it, argue with it, sometimes improve it, sometimes simply recycle it. Very little appears out of nowhere. Most things we proudly call new are often just older ideas wearing better clothes.

What one generation treats as sacred, the next generation edits, alters, and reshapes to suit its own moment. Traditions bend, meanings shift, and ideas slowly pick up new shapes as they pass through different hands. Creative work has always moved like this. Artists look at what came before them, borrow from it, argue with it, sometimes improve it, sometimes simply recycle it. Very little appears out of nowhere. Most things we proudly call new are often just older ideas wearing better clothes.

body.html: Better clothes. Who does not like them? The same idea appears quite clearly in design, especially in the world of UX and UI. Spend enough time looking at digital products and the similarities start to show. The same navigation bars, the same card layouts, the same buttons appearing again and again across different platforms. Even when the product is new, the interface rarely feels unfamiliar. Like the outfit repeater debate. Everyone frowns upon it, yet most wardrobes run on it. Design is not very different. Are designers creating something new, or just giving old ideas better clothes?

Like the outfit repeater debate. Everyone frowns upon it, yet most wardrobes run on it. Design is not very different. Are designers creating something new, or just giving old ideas better clothes?

body.html: In many ways, this repetition is not accidental. Design depends on familiarity. A button should look like a button, not something people have to pause and figure out. A menu should clearly tell customers what food is available, not confuse them with stylish calligraphy. Interfaces work best when people understand them instantly. Users arrive with expectations. They assume things will behave in ways they have already learned elsewhere. When designers follow those expectations, the experience feels smooth and natural. Not every corner of design needs a state of the art evolution. Sometimes the smartest choice is to keep things simple and familiar.

body.text: Interlocking Monograms across luxury brands - Chanel's CC and Gucci's GG

body.html: And because familiarity matters so much, designers rarely begin from absolute scratch. Much of the design world already runs on shared structures that people recognize. Tools like Figma and Wix openly provide templates, components, and readymade layouts. Things like navigation bars, cards, grids, and buttons appear again and again across products because people already know how to use them. Designers step in, arrange these pieces, adapt them, and shape them around the needs of a product. The work is not about inventing every element from nothing. It is about knowing how to use what already exists well.

body.html: This pattern may sound extremely similar to T.S Eliot’s essay ‘Tradition and Individual Talent”. Eliot argued that tradition is never separate from the present. Every new work grows out of what already exists. The past does not disappear, it just shapes the present. What we call originality is just tradition, slightly rearranged.

Designers simply refine them, adapt them, and make them work better. Sometimes originality is not invention. It is simply knowing what deserves to be repeated.

blogPosts.title: Design and the Question of Authority
blogPosts.subtitle: Design has always been an act of interpretation. What happens when AI begins to share that role?

body.html: Design is power because it is interpretation. To design is to decide what is central and what is peripheral. That authority has largely belonged to humans. It may not for much longer.
body.text: Design is power because it is interpretation. To design is to decide what is central and what is peripheral. That authority has largely belonged to humans. It may not for much longer.

body.html: This is not a rejection of progress. The world is moving fast. Artificial intelligence now designs interfaces, writes code, builds systems, and makes decisions in seconds. It consumes energy and water at scale to do so. And we call that efficiency. The same human mind that once questioned God during the Renaissance now asks algorithms what to write, what to choose, what to think. We fought wars. We built nations. Now we outsource judgement. Speed has increased. Authority is slipping.
body.text: This is not a rejection of progress. The world is moving fast. Artificial intelligence now designs interfaces, writes code, builds systems, and makes decisions in seconds. It consumes energy and water at scale to do so. And we call that efficiency. The same human mind that once questioned God during the Renaissance now asks algorithms what to write, what to choose, what to think. We fought wars. We built nations. Now we outsource judgement. Speed has increased. Authority is slipping.

body.html: And authority has slipped before. During the Renaissance, humans began to question divine power and reconsider their place in the hierarchy of the world. The idea that authority could be examined, even challenged, took hold. Art reflected that shift. In The Creation of Adam, Adam does not kneel or shrink. He meets God at eye level. The space between them is narrow.  Meaning is no longer untouchable. It is open to human interpretation.

The idea that authority could be examined, even challenged, took hold. Art reflected that shift. In The Creation of Adam, Adam does not kneel or shrink. He meets God at eye level. The space between them is narrow.  Meaning is no longer untouchable. It is open to human interpretation.

body.html: If the Renaissance brought interpretation into human hands, the AI era is quietly taking it back. Algorithms decide what ranks first, what gets seen, what is suggested, what disappears. They influence decisions before humans realise a decision has been shaped. We call it progress. We rarely call it power. But when machines interpret the world for us, humans are no longer the final authority.

body.html: If AI can interpret, generate, and build systems on its own, what keeps designers relevant? When algorithms decide the order, draft the layout, and shape the flow, humans step back. The structure is set before the designer begins. The designer edits what the system has already created. When machines interpret, they hold part of the power.

body.html: If Renaissance was a moment when humans claimed authority over meaning, then the AI era asks a harder question. What happens when interpretation is no longer only human? What is left for humans when systems make the decisions? Is this another shift in power, or the start of something else? The destabilisation has begun. Where it leads is still unclear.

body.html: There is no standard rulebook to create good design, else every design would look the same. While it is important to follow rhythms and think of design analytically, we must also remember to make our design human (breaking rules where we deem necessary). I would argue that most web design currently look same because the thought leaders at big tech have all created easily accessible design systems, making it easier for us to rip off of them. However, this results in design that looks suspiciously similar to everything else that exits on the web.

blogPosts.title: Mobile First Design: Why Most Websites Fail on Phones
blogPosts.subtitle: Most websites are designed for desktop but used on mobile. Understand the design gaps that impact usability, performance, and user retention.

body.html: Desktop Design vs Mobile Reality
body.text: Desktop Design vs Mobile Reality

body.html: Most websites are not designed for how people actually use them. They are built for large screens, full attention, and precise interaction. That is not how users show up anymore. They are on smaller screens, switching between tasks, making quick decisions. When design ignores this, it does not matter how good it looks. It fails in use.
body.text: Most websites are not designed for how people actually use them. They are built for large screens, full attention, and precise interaction. That is not how users show up anymore. They are on smaller screens, switching between tasks, making quick decisions. When design ignores this, it does not matter how good it looks. It fails in use.

body.html: Most websites are designed for desktops but used on phones. They assume users will read everything, click accurately, and take their time. What works with a mouse does not work on touch. What looks clear on a large screen feels crowded on a small one. Users leave.

body.html: Common Mobile UX Failures
body.text: Common Mobile UX Failures

body.html: Many websites are not built for mobile first use. Layouts break, text becomes hard to read, and navigation gets unclear. Menus become complex, buttons get smaller, and key actions become harder to find. On a small screen, that is enough to lose users.
body.text: Many websites are not built for mobile first use. Layouts break, text becomes hard to read, and navigation gets unclear. Menus become complex, buttons get smaller, and key actions become harder to find. On a small screen, that is enough to lose users.

body.html: Content adds to the problem. Long paragraphs, small fonts, and too many elements compete for attention. Users do not process all of it. They scroll past and miss key information.
body.text: Content adds to the problem. Long paragraphs, small fonts, and too many elements compete for attention. Users do not process all of it. They scroll past and miss key information.

body.html: Pages that take more than a few seconds to load lose users before they start. Speed directly impacts whether users stay or leave. This happens because most websites are not tested in real conditions. Different devices, screen sizes, and network speeds reveal issues that do not show up on a desktop.

This happens because most websites are not tested in real conditions. Different devices, screen sizes, and network speeds reveal issues that do not show up on a desktop.

body.html: How Users Actually Interact on Mobile
body.text: How Users Actually Interact on Mobile

body.html: Users do not use websites in ideal conditions. They are moving, multitasking, and checking things quickly. Attention is limited, but decision speed is high. As noted by Steve Jobs, mobile introduced a constraint. Interfaces need to work on small screens, often used with one hand, in motion, and understood within seconds. What appears at the top of the screen gets seen first, and often only. Content below the fold is often not seen. This forces prioritisation of what appears first. A common user observation on Reddit highlights the same constraint. Smaller screens force designers to focus on what matters while keeping the rest discoverable. This leads to simpler flows and less complexity. Interaction is physical. Most usage is one handed. The thumb does the work. The bottom of the screen is easier to reach, while top corners require more effort. Actions placed there slow users down. Touch is less precise and has no hover. Small targets and tight spacing increase errors. Desktop patterns do not translate directly. Users decide quickly if something is relevant, useful, and worth continuing. If not, they move on. If a website does not work in real conditions, it does not work. Context matters more than layout. Most websites still ignore it.

body.html: While watching films, I have often noticed how much room the director gives a scene to breathe. Some moments are allowed to sit with you, and others are cut short to keep the story moving. Over time, this made me more aware of pacing in web design. In website design, we often move quickly from idea to execution. When that pace becomes constant, the space to experiment tends to shrink.

blogPosts.title: The subtle art of choosing typography and how to approach it.
blogPosts.subtitle: We spend a lot of time picking fonts, but not enough time thinking about how they are read. What changes when typography is chosen for clarity instead of style?

body.html: When I think of choosing typography, I think of a craft similar to choosing a plate for a meal. Think fried chicken served in a white plate vs fried chicken wrapped in a newspaper. The plate or the newspaper does not determine how the chicken will taste. But it will determine in what context the chicken should be consumed.
body.text: When I think of choosing typography, I think of a craft similar to choosing a plate for a meal. Think fried chicken served in a white plate vs fried chicken wrapped in a newspaper. The plate or the newspaper does not determine how the chicken will taste. But it will determine in what context the chicken should be consumed.

body.html: Historically, fonts were developed to make copies of written text at large scale — a revolutionary invention of its time. But as centuries passed by and copying became a widespread phenomenon, fonts took over a more complex role. The job of typography today is to be the vessel for the content that's being presented, in addition to bringing attention to itself. Think about every time you stumble upon a beautifully designed website and wonder why it felt so easy to read!

Think about every time you stumble upon a beautifully designed website and wonder why it felt so easy to read!

body.html: The skill of choosing typography is an abstract one and the millions of fonts available online doesn't make the job any easier. But, we can still think of a few basic principles to keep in mind.

body.html: 1. Understand the content first.

body.html: 5. How many fonts must we choose ?

body.html: Understanding the scope of our design project is important. How much written content must we accommodate and what is the purpose of the application or website we are designing for. If our website spans 100s of pages with different contexts, we will always be safer in choosing different styles from a same family. If our project has a smaller scope, say a microsite, we can perhaps play around with numerous fonts.

If our website spans 100s of pages with different contexts, we will always be safer in choosing different styles from a same family. If our project has a smaller scope, say a microsite, we can perhaps play around with numerous fonts.

body.html: In my opinion though, less is always better. One is acceptable, two is excellent. Use 3 when 2 might not be enough.

body.html: We must not stress the audience with the trouble of remembering multiple fonts. But we must also not be happy with obvious choices. The correct balance will always be in its nuance.

body.html: Conclusion.
body.text: Conclusion.

body.html: The correct way to approach choosing typography for any design project should always be content first. All fonts have unique features, but these visual features are just ornamentation if they have nothing to say. Just like the job of the newspaper or the plate is to bring attention to the fried chicken served, our job is to choose the correct vessel for the content. We become better at it every time we take steps to understand, analyze and think about what’s being written.

blogPosts.title: What is px? What is a pt? What is dp?
blogPosts.subtitle: iOS’ design measures in pts, Androids in dp, and design for the web is done in px but what do they mean and what is the difference?

body.html: Pixel
body.text: Pixel

body.html: ‘Pixel’ is the abbreviation of the word Picture Element (Pi x El ). It is the smallest square block (element) of color that forms an image on a screen.
body.text: ‘Pixel’ is the abbreviation of the word Picture Element (Pi x El ). It is the smallest square block (element) of color that forms an image on a screen.

body.html: Note: Pixels need not be squares as they can be rendered as lines and dots too.
body.text: Note: Pixels need not be squares as they can be rendered as lines and dots too.

body.html: Up until 2010, a pixel meant a pixel, it was measurable and life was easy.
body.text: Up until 2010, a pixel meant a pixel, it was measurable and life was easy.

body.html: Before the iPhone 4’s retina display, the number of pixels that could fit on a square area of 1 inch was 163 pixels. It was fixed or at least was the standard.
body.text: Before the iPhone 4’s retina display, the number of pixels that could fit on a square area of 1 inch was 163 pixels. It was fixed or at least was the standard.

body.html: All that changed when the iPhone introduced retina display. An inch of a retina display could now house 326 pixels. And as it is a convention, other companies started following suit with crazy pixel counts included per inch of screen.
body.text: All that changed when the iPhone introduced retina display. An inch of a retina display could now house 326 pixels. And as it is a convention, other companies started following suit with crazy pixel counts included per inch of screen.

body.html: Here’s where all the problem started-
body.text: Here’s where all the problem started-

body.html: Say you designed a button 2 pixels high and 4 pixels wide, the size would now vary hugely depending if your website or app is viewed on a phone screen with 163 pixels per inch or 326 pixels per inch display. You would now have to make the design over and over again every time for a range of devices with the same sizes, let alone different aspect ratios.
body.text: Say you designed a button 2 pixels high and 4 pixels wide, the size would now vary hugely depending if your website or app is viewed on a phone screen with 163 pixels per inch or 326 pixels per inch display. You would now have to make the design over and over again every time for a range of devices with the same sizes, let alone different aspect ratios.

body.html: Apple solved this problem by introducing the Point (pt)
body.text: Apple solved this problem by introducing the Point (pt)

body.html: A point was defined to be exactly equal to a pixel when it was viewed on the original iPhone. i.e 1 px = 1 pt when viewed on a screen of density 163 pixels/inch. As different versions of the iPhone came with different screen resolutions, iOS would then internally convert the points to pixels to make a button look the same size no matter how many pixels fit in an inch of the screen.

blogPosts.title: Why a Button Can Be Patented, But a Heritage Can’t
blogPosts.subtitle: Why can UX elements be patented while cultural designs remain unprotected? A look at ownership, attribution, and design law

body.html: Culture cannot be patented.
body.text: Culture cannot be patented.

body.html: That is what allows Chanel, Dior, Ralph Lauren and Louis Vuitton to use Indian design elements across collections without attribution. Jhumkas, textiles, embroidery. The reference is clear. The credit is not.
body.text: That is what allows Chanel, Dior, Ralph Lauren and Louis Vuitton to use Indian design elements across collections without attribution. Jhumkas, textiles, embroidery. The reference is clear. The credit is not.

body.html:
So the question is simple:
Why do these brands get to use Indian design without credit?
body.text:
So the question is simple:

body.html: In digital design, brands are not allowed to use design elements freely without consequences. Ownership is defined. There are legal systems that decide what can be protected and who it belongs to. Specific elements, interactions, and patterns can be claimed. A button, a gesture, even the way something responds on screen can fall under intellectual property.
body.text: In digital design, brands are not allowed to use design elements freely without consequences. Ownership is defined. There are legal systems that decide what can be protected and who it belongs to. Specific elements, interactions, and patterns can be claimed. A button, a gesture, even the way something responds on screen can fall under intellectual property.

body.html: Using someone else’s design without permission is not just questionable. It can be challenged, restricted, and enforced.
body.text: Using someone else’s design without permission is not just questionable. It can be challenged, restricted, and enforced.

body.html: If a company creates a specific way something works on a website, they can claim it. How a page responds, how elements move, how users navigate. If it is new and clearly defined, it can be registered.
body.text: If a company creates a specific way something works on a website, they can claim it. How a page responds, how elements move, how users navigate. If it is new and clearly defined, it can be registered.

body.html: That is what makes it enforceable. Once it is registered, others cannot freely copy it. If they do, there are consequences.
body.text: That is what makes it enforceable. Once it is registered, others cannot freely copy it. If they do, there are consequences.

body.html: This is not just about legal systems. It is also how designers approach their work. As one user on Quora notes, much of UI and UX is shared by default. Patterns repeat, interactions feel familiar, and designers build on what already exists.
body.text: This is not just about legal systems. It is also how designers approach their work. As one user on Quora notes, much of UI and UX is shared by default. Patterns repeat, interactions feel familiar, and designers build on what already exists.

body.html: Ownership only applies when something is specific enough to be claimed.
body.text: Ownership only applies when something is specific enough to be claimed.

body.html: Even within Indian law, protection has limits. The Designs Act, 2000 allows a design to be registered only if it is new and tied to a specific creator. It protects form, not origin. Which means cultural designs do not really fit into this system. They are not new. They are not owned by one person. So they remain unprotected.

Which means cultural designs do not really fit into this system. They are not new. They are not owned by one person. So they remain unprotected.

body.html: So the difference is not just about design. It is about what the system chooses to recognize as ownership. In one case, something new can be defined, claimed, and protected. In the other, something that has always existed remains open to use without obligation.

body.html: The difference is clear. What is new can be owned. What has always existed cannot.

blogPosts.title: What should be the size of an icon button?
blogPosts.subtitle: Buttons are everywhere. And yet we see an overabundance of "bad buttons". So, how to resolve that?

body.html: In our very first article, we try to explore the comfortable range of sizes in which designers can experiment with the size of icon buttons. We also dive into how size can be used to guide users to the most favorable actions.
body.text: In our very first article, we try to explore the comfortable range of sizes in which designers can experiment with the size of icon buttons. We also dive into how size can be used to guide users to the most favorable actions.

body.html: 1. Touch Target
body.text: 1. Touch Target

body.html: Interaction with buttons on desktops (and to a large extent on laptops) are done using mouse cursors. Hence button sizes could possibly be smaller. The problem arises when we encounter touchscreens. We use our fingers to interact with touch screens. Thus the size of our fingertips (index finger and thumb) decides how small an icon button could possibly be to effectively serve its purpose.
body.text: Interaction with buttons on desktops (and to a large extent on laptops) are done using mouse cursors. Hence button sizes could possibly be smaller. The problem arises when we encounter touchscreens. We use our fingers to interact with touch screens. Thus the size of our fingertips (index finger and thumb) decides how small an icon button could possibly be to effectively serve its purpose.

body.html: An MIT study found that the average width of an index finger is 45–57 px and the avg size of the thumb is 72 px.

body.html: 2. Touch Accuracy
